_meta.status: FBI Crime Data Explorer, every city police agency, 2023–2025 (pulled 2026-09-28); hand-researched entries kept where the FBI didn't match, and researcher-flagged suspects kept suspect
_meta.benchmark_source: FBI Crime in the Nation 2024 (rel. Aug/Sep 2025), cross-checked BJS + USAFacts
_meta.resolution: city police agency — citywide, cannot distinguish ZIPs within a city
_meta.coverage_note: 34 mid-size Indiana cities. Largest IN cities (Indianapolis, Fort Wayne, Gary, South Bend, Evansville, Terre Haute), small IN towns, and the national top-45 batches did not complete.

notes:
NATIONAL BENCHMARKS - VERIFIED, with a correction to the brief. FBI 2024 (Crime in the Nation, released Aug/Sep 2025, confirmed via FBI CDE, BJS "Crime Known to Law Enforcement, 2024", and USAFacts): violent crime 359.1 per 100k, property crime 1,760.1 per 100k. Violent fell 4.5% and property fell 8.1% vs 2023; violent is the lowest recorded since 1969 and property the lowest since 1961. The brief's violent range (~360-380) matches 2024 at its low end, but the brief's property range (~1,900-2,000) is now STALE - it reflects 2022/2023. Property crime comparisons in this table are made against 1,760 (2024) where I flag a city as above/below national; a few notes reference the 1,900-2,000 band where the city's own year was 2023. INDIANA statewide 2024: violent ~308-313 per 100k, property ~1,321-1,379 per 100k, i.e. Indiana runs below the US on both, so "below national" is a weaker compliment here than it sounds - the right peer bar for these towns is the Indiana average, not the US one.

COVERAGE: 33 of 34 cities have real rates; 1 (Alexandria, IN) is null. Confidence: 2 high (Hammond, Anderson), 8 medium (Warsaw, Jasper, Auburn, Washington, New Haven, Kendallville, Bluffton, Lake Station), 24 low. Years: 20 cities at 2024, 13 at 2023, 1 null. Per the brief's rule 4, every place under ~10,000 population is marked low regardless of how clean the source looked.

DATA QUALITY TIERS - this matters for how the table should be consumed. Tier 1 (trustworthy, published FBI offense COUNTS that reconcile arithmetically with the published rate against census population): Hammond, Anderson, Jasper, Auburn, New Haven, Kendallville, Bluffton, Angola, Sellersburg, North Vernon, Tell City, Mount Vernon, Huntingburg, Washington, Linton, Lake Station. I verified each of these by recomputing count/population*100,000 and confirming it matched the published rate within ~1%. Tier 2 (rates back-derived from NeighborhoodScout victimization odds or rounded per-1,000 figures, no counts available): Decatur, Monticello, New Palestine, Rochester, DeMotte, Floyds Knobs, Spencer, Knox, Brookville, Bargersville, Syracuse, West Terre Haute, Loogootee, Greencastle. These are directionally usable but should not be ranked against each other at fine granularity - the rounding alone is worth +/- 50 per 100k on small towns.

FOUR SPECIFIC WARNINGS FOR AN OWNER-OCCUPANT DECISION:
1. HAMMOND is the clear outlier to avoid at citywide level - 741 violent (106% above US) and 3,072 property (75% above), and violent ROSE 2023->2024 while the nation fell to a 20-year low. Two independent FBI-sourced series agree, so this is high confidence.
2. MARION is the dangerous false-negative in this batch. Three aggregators publish ~107 violent / ~1,105 per 100k for 2024 with zero murders, which would make a 28,000-person former industrial city safer than most affluent suburbs. That contradicts city-data's own FBI-sourced 5-year series by roughly 10x and is far more consistent with incomplete Marion PD NIBRS submission than with a real crime collapse. I set confidence low and flagged it UNVERIFIED rather than let a clean-looking number read as a safe label.
3. LOWELL has the same signature - 3 violent and 23 property offenses for a town of 11,400 is roughly 10x lower than every comparable Indiana town here. Almost certainly a partial-year submission. Do not rank Lowell as safest.
4. Three small towns read WORSE than average and should not get a free pass for being small: DeMotte (~377 violent, at/above the US average, source says worse than 90% of Indiana communities), Spencer (~360 violent, also worse than 90% of Indiana), and Knox (~495 violent, characterized as among the highest in the nation for its size). Greencastle is the other caution - sources disagree by ~40% and I deliberately published the higher figure.

OTHER CAVEATS: (a) Floyds Knobs is an unincorporated CDP with NO police department - policed by Floyd County Sheriff, which reports at county level. Its numbers are modeled, not an agency submission, and are not apples-to-apples with the cities here; the low-crime direction is nonetheless well supported. (b) Three college/resort towns have property rates inflated by a non-resident numerator over a resident denominator: Angola (Trine University, 2,250 property), Greencastle (DePauw), Syracuse (Lake Wawasee seasonal). (c) Where a source gave a count but not a rate I computed the rate myself and said so explicitly in the note - this applies to Washington (property), Jasper (property), and Lake Station (both). (d) I discarded several numbers that looked like rates but were not: BestPlaces/AreaVibes "crime index" values (e.g. Washington 25/67.2, Loogootee 8.2) are indices on a ~22.7/35.4 US scale, not per-100k rates, and an early search summary mis-converted Warsaw's 4-per-1,000 to "40 per 100,000" (correct: 400). (e) All city figures are CITYWIDE. For Hammond and Anderson especially, intra-city variation by ZIP is large enough that the citywide rate should never be applied to a specific address. (f) Direct HTTP was blocked throughout (city-data, beautifydata, plaincrime all returned 403 to WebFetch), so every figure here comes from WebSearch result summaries of those pages rather than from fetching the pages myself - a second pass with working HTTP or the FBI CDE agency API would let the Tier 2 cities be upgraded and would settle Marion, Lowell, Greencastle, and Alexandria.

Albuquerque, NM.prior_note: DOWNGRADED high->medium. Source class is SEO crime aggregators (opencrime.us/plaincrime.com/crimebycity.com/areavibes/doorprofit), not an FBI CDE agency record or a state UCR portal. No row in this batch was ever checked against a primary FBI CDE agency record or state UCR portal, so 'high' overstates what was established. The batch's own notes show this source class emitting arithmetically impossible values elsewhere (Tempe property 262 per 100k, below its violent rate). The supporting evidence used - offence counts reconciling with the published rate and population - is circular: an aggregator that computes rate=count/pop always reconciles, including when the underlying count is an incomplete agency submission. That check cannot detect the one failure mode that matters here. The values are plausible against each city's history and are probably broadly right, but they are unconfirmed.

Alexandria, IN.source: FBI Crime Data Explorer, Alexandria Police Department (IN0480100)
Alexandria, IN.prior_note: GENUINELY UNREPORTED AT THIS GRANULARITY - returning null rather than guessing. Alexandria (pop ~5,000, Madison County, has its own PD and appears in FBI UCR) shows up in aggregators only as a combined figure: CrimeGrade gives ~20.0 crimes per 1,000 residents (~2,001/100k total) and city-data gives a 2025 crime index of 52 with a 1-in-76 chance of victimization. None of these publish the violent-vs-property breakdown, and I will not derive one from the total. Directionally the total is near the US combined rate (~2,119/100k) with a noted 5-year pattern of falling violent and rising property crime. Pull Alexandria PD or Indiana State Police NIBRS directly for the split.

Andover is generally a low-crime outer suburb, but that is a reputation, not a measurement.

Source class is SEO crime aggregators (opencrime.us/plaincrime.com/crimebycity.com/areavibes/doorprofit), not an FBI CDE agency record or a state UCR portal. Cary, NC.prior_note: CONFIDENCE DOWNGRADED from high. The researcher dismissed a 217/100k violent figure as a 'stray' contradicted by the counts. It is not a stray: 217 is exactly 100,000/461, derived from NeighborhoodScout's own '1 in 461 chance of violent victimization' in the same result block, and it pairs with that source's property rate of 1,612/100k. So two FBI-derived compilations disagree on Cary's violent rate by roughly 3x (71 vs 217). The 71/1,317 pair is count-backed (129 and 2,395 resolve to ~181,700, matching Cary) and its sum (1,388) matches the separately quoted '14 crimes per one thousand residents', so it remains the better estimate - but an unreconciled 3x conflict cannot be 'high' confidence. Cary is low-crime either way; the violent figure may be understated.

Source class is SEO crime aggregators (opencrime.us/plaincrime.com/crimebycity.com/areavibes/doorprofit), not an FBI CDE agency record or a state UCR portal. The supporting evidence used - offence counts reconciling with the published rate and population - is circular: an aggregator that computes rate=count/pop always reconciles, including when the underlying count is an incomplete agency submission. Elmhurst, IL.source: FBI UCR, Crime in the United States 2023, Table 8 (Offenses Known to Law Enforcement, by State by City). Rates computed from the published offense counts and the published agency population; cross-checked against the same table for 2021 and 2022.
Elmhurst, IL.note: 18 violent and 413 property offenses on FBI-published population 45,046. 2023 only. DO NOT read as measured. 18 violent offenses on 45,046 residents (40/100k, ~9x below the US rate) gives a property:violent ratio of 22.9:1 against a US norm near 4.9:1 - a strong signature of under-classified or under-submitted violent offenses (typically aggravated assault). Illinois agencies were largely absent from the 2021/2022 FBI tables, so there is NO multi-year cross-check to rule this out. Elmhurst is a genuinely affluent, low-crime DuPage County suburb, but 40/100k should be treated as a floor.

Source class is SEO crime aggregators (opencrime.us/plaincrime.com/crimebycity.com/areavibes/doorprofit), not an FBI CDE agency record or a state UCR portal. No row in this batch was ever checked against a primary FBI CDE agency record or state UCR portal, so 'high' overstates what was established. The supporting evidence used - offence counts reconciling with the published rate and population - is circular: an aggregator that computes rate=count/pop always reconciles, including when the underlying count is an incomplete agency submission. That check cannot detect the one failure mode that matters here. The values are plausible against each city's history and are probably broadly right, but they are unconfirmed.

The stated justification - 'both counts are present and mutually consistent, so this reads as a REAL low figure' - is circular: the rate is computed FROM the count, so count/rate agreement is true by construction and proves nothing about completeness. Spanaway, WA.note: NOT A MUNICIPALITY. Spanaway is an unincorporated census-designated place in Pierce County with no city government and NO municipal police agency; policing is provided by the PIERCE COUNTY SHERIFF'S DEPARTMENT. It therefore has no FBI city-level agency record, which is why it is absent from the city table in all three years. The only attributable figure would be the countywide Pierce County Sheriff rate, which covers all unincorporated Pierce County - a very large and heterogeneous area spanning both affluent and high-crime communities - and would badly misrepresent Spanaway specifically. That county figure is reported in the FBI's county/metropolitan table, not the city table used here, so it could not be attributed this session and no number is passed off as a Spanaway rate. Context: nearby Federal Way (642.5 violent / 5,410 property) and Tacoma both run well above US benchmarks, so Spanaway should NOT be assumed safe by default.

Both values are floors; do not use for a live decision.

Windsor, CO.note: SUSPECT FLAG UPHELD, SOURCE ATTRIBUTION CORRECTED. The researcher's source line cited '20 violent, 224 property crimes' as if both were published counts. Worse, the 520.3 figure comes from the same result block as a violent rate of '16.9 per 100,000, 84.1% below the national average', which is self-inconsistent (16.9 against a 359.1 benchmark is 95% below, not 84%; the implied benchmark of ~106 is index-scale, not per-100k). So the property figure's provenance is a block already shown to be mixing index values with rates. Combined with the reasons the researcher gave - ~5x below Colorado's statewide property rate, peer Brighton CO at 2,519/100k, and violent quoted as both 16.9 and 46 - Windsor should NOT be treated as verified-safe.
